speechtext: FIELDING (Minister of Finance) moved that the House go into Committee of Supply.

Mr. Speaker, before you leave the chair, I would like to ask the Prime Minister if he has any information to communicate to the House with reference to the movements of Sir Elzear Taschereau? Before the House adjourned this morning I took the opportunity of calling the attention of the Finance Minister who was leading the House to a cablegram which appeared in the ' Montreal Star ' of yesterday announcing that His Lordship had left London suddenly and intended to sail by the steamship ' Ionian.' Is the right hon. gentleman aware that he has left London suddenly ; and, if so, what is the reason ? Has he been recalled ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have no information whatever.
Have the government made any inquiry as to the remarks of Chief Justice Taschereau, as they did in the case of Lord Dundonald ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There is a difference between the position held by the Chief Justice and that held by Lord Dundonald. We asked Lord Dundonald in regard to the remarks he had made, as he was an official of ours. Sir Elzear Taschereau is not an official of this government.
When are the final supplementary estimates to toe brought down ? Is there any other legislation to be brought down than that on the order paper?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I stated yesterday that I hoped the estimates might be down to-day, but I am inclined to think they will not be down until Monday.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is not contemplated to bring in any more legislation.
I see a report in the papers that a Bill is to be introduced in reference to superannuation in connection with the Intercolonial Railway.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
As to that I cannot say in the absence of the Minister of Railways. There may be some departmental measures, but it is not intended to toring anything of a contentious nature.
Mr. SiPROULE. At this stage I think we ought to have some information from the government in regard to the Bills on the order paper which they intend to put through and those which they intend to drop. It is rumoured that it is not the intention of the government to put them all through. Can the Prime Minister give us any information on that point ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
On Monday next my hon. friend the Minister of Finance Mr. FIELDING.
intends to bring down the estimates. Then we shall have practically everything we intend to bring down during the present session, unless some measures of a non-contentious character ; and then if my hon. friend is in a mood to go home as much as I am, we may give him some information and perhaps be guided by his intention.
It is not the opposition that is running the House, but the government.

In the absence of the chairman of the Committee on Banking and Commerce, I beg to ask the Minister of Finance if he can inform the House when we may expect another meeting of that committee ? There is still one important Bill undisposed of, and it is very desirable that the committee should meet at an early day in order to finish up the business.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am afraid I am not able to give my hon. friend any information on the subject. I was under the impression that the business of the Banking and Commerce Committee was completed. There is one Bill, I understand, which has not been disposed of ; but I was informed, as I believe my hon. friend has been, that that Bill was not to be proceeded with. If that be the case, I do not see any need of calling, the committee. I have no objection to it being called, tout I have no information of what the intention of the chairman is. 1 am inclined to think that the promoter does not intend to proceed with the Bill.
I may say that while the promoter may not intend to proceed writh it, possibly the committee may.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will take the responsibility of saying, as one member of the committee, that as it is a private Bill, if the promoter does not want to proceed with it, 1 do not see how anybody else can have any interest in pressing it. .
It is in the hands of the committee.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: When we had this item up before, the minister promised to bring down a statement showing the reason for the discrepancy of about $20,000 between his report and the report of the Auditor General as to the expenditure on experimental farms.

When this matter was up before, the hon. gentleman pointed out what appeared to be a discrepancy between the
statements in the Auditor General's Report and the statement at the end of the farm

report of this year, on page 429. The Auditor General's Report at page D-36 gives a statement of the expenditure on the Central Experimental Farm, amounting to $55,205.60. The discrepancy that appears is due to the following : The salaries of the officers at the central farm are charged in the Auditor General's Report all to the Central Farm, but in the experimental farm detailed expenditure the salaries of the director, $4,000 ; accountant, $758.31 ; assistant accountant, $416.65 ; stenographer, $800 ; amounting to $5,974.96, are divided amongst the different farms in the ratio of thirty per cent to the Central Experimental Farm and 174 per cent ($1,045.62) to each of the other farms. This makes a total of $4,182.47 to be deducted from the items in the Auditor General's Report. In the botanical and entomological division 30 per cent is charged to the central farm and 17J per cent to each of the others. This division is charged $3,787.56 in the Auditor General's Report. The salaries of Messrs. Fletcher, Guignard and Gibson are comprised in this figure with some other slight expenditures. The total of the four parts charged to the branch farms is $2,345, which deducted leaves $1,442.56 charged to the central farm. The chemical division is divided in the same way. The salaries of Messrs. Shutt, Charlton and the other gentlemen amount to $4,100, and the additional expenses make a total of $4,706.86 in the Auditor General's Report, out of which $3,296.76 is charged to the branch farms leaving $1,410.10. The travelling expenses are the same in both cases. There are a number of small items of freight on exhibition supplies at Nappan and charged to central farm in error amounting to 35 cents to be deducted and $120 for value of grain for exhibitors to be added. The telegrams and telephones are not divided and they amount to $144.06. In office help, &c., there was a proportion of office help charged for the distribution of seed grain as marked on the vouchers, which the Auditor General through some error charged to the central farm. That item comes to $4,018.71 instead of $4,543.71. In printing, stationery, newspapers, and periodicals, cost of money orders for chemicals, payment of chemicals, supplies and seed, instead of being $109.09 should be $104.35. In seed-grain, trees, &c., we have to add to the Auditor General's figures 97 cents and for freight on seeds from Ottawa to Nappan chargeable to Nappan $1.20, we have to deduct from the Auditor General's figures which will make that item $446.21 instead of $446.44. The horticultural division is the same in both, viz., $5,110.92. In the distribution of seed grain, trees, office help, &c., there was $525 ; for office help, $125.48 value of grain supplied by Brandon Farm ; $712.64 value of grain supplied by Indiau Head Farm, $438.43 supplied by central farm, less screenings used for seed, $334.55, leaving* the difference of $1,467 which ought to be added to the Auditor General's figures making it $6,029.56, instead of $4,562.56. The farm report shows $5,871.82 to which is to be added $157.74 for the distribution of seed, and the two lumped together make $6,029.o6 exactly the figures which appear in the Auditor General's Report. Under seed testing, and care of green houses, &c., the cost of taking meteorological observations is charged in the farm account as contingencies has to be deducted from that item in the Auditor General's Report. The reason of this is that the man who takes charge of the green houses is paid for the meteorological observations. The Auditor General has put that in with seed testing and care of green houses, whereas in the farm report it is charged to contingencies. The item in the Auditor General's Report is $1,091.39. the same item in the farm report being $1,019.39. If you subtract the $72 from the Auditor General's Report it brings it down to the $1,019.39. The item for arboretum, forestry, and care of grounds is the same in each report. In live stock the value of one short horn bull sent from Ottawa to Agassiz $350, is to be deducted from the Auditor General's figures, leaving the balance, $1,146.08. This was credited to the central farm stock in the Auditor General's figures. In farm work, &c., as the division of cereal breeding, &c., had only been in operation for a portion of the year, the expenses were included in this item and they amount to $2,805.47. There was also a small charge for services in London, England, of $25.54, making the item altogether in the Auditor General's Report, $7,913.36. There was credited in the Auditor General's Report to the Central Experimental Farm, for feed supply to poultry, and various other items amounting to $1,072.52, which deducted from $7,913.36, leaves $6,840.84 the exact item that appears in the report. For draining implements, blacksmithing and harness supplies, manure and fertilizers and dairy department, the items are the same. In the poultry department the value of feed suplied from the farm $218.59 ought to be added to $1,773.45, which makes $1,992.04, the exact item in the farm report. In Bee supplies the item is the same.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has produced a large number of figures showing divisions and subdivisions to account for the discrepancies, but I say to you Mr. Chairman and to this committee that neither he nor any other person can account for it in any other way than by saying that the statement which he has published and sent out bo the country is not a fair statement. The hon. gentleman has made some very strong statements.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Very correct statements, which required strong language.
And this the hon. gentleman is master of. He has quoted from the Auditor General's Report, and I accept as correct the figures which he has taken from that report.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Then you will accept my whole statement as correct ?

No, figures and deductions from figures are two different things. The hon. gentleman quoted the Auditor General's Report, which is divided into sections, and section D is applied to the Department of Agriculture. In that section there are many figures which correspond exactly with those in the departmental report. Then the hon. gentleman went to the section which is devoted to public works and took a lot of items out of that department.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Was that not expenditure in connection with the experimental farm ?

They are expenditures of the Public Works Department in connection, it is true, with the experimental farm.
Mr. TAYLOR, You could not run a farm without them.
Perhaps not.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Then you should have added to your account that expenditure.
I have followed the method adopted toy the Auditor General and prefer his plan to that of my hon. friend.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The Auditor General's Report has nothing to do with the report of the Department of Agriculture.

If my hon. friend will only keep cool, I will be able to explain the matter to him. He has become confused by figures from two different parts of the Auditor General's report. I prefer following the lines of the division of expenditure adopted by the Auditor General, and I have kept to them and have put into the farm report the figures which the Auditor General has embraced under the heading ' D,' which applies to agriculture. I have not gone through the whole of the other departments to find out whether there are in them any figures which might possibly be twisted into subserviency of my work. The hon. gentleman is aware of the fact that the Public Works Department deals with the public buildings of the Dominion. It takes care of the post offices. It pays for the heating, lighting, management and repairs to post offices, but these are not charged against the administration of the Post Office Department by the Auditor General. The Public Works Department deals with the care of custom offices all over the country, and it heats, lights and repairs them and pays the caretaker.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: When the Minister of Customs or the Postmaster General can seek to contrast the revenue of their departments with the cost of running those departments do they show every item of cost ?

They do not. What I have done in that respect is exactly what the Post Office Department and the Customs Department do. The Post 'Office Department does not charge itself with the expense of caretaking, heating or lighting the post office buildings. Nor does the Customs Department charge itself with these items in connection with the custom house. Nor does the Auditor General charge these departments with the expenditures made by the Public Works Department in connection with these buildings any more than he charges such expenditures against the experimental farms. And the hon. gentleman has proved that toy going to the Auditor General's statement and actually taking the Mr. TAYLOR.
figures from the accounts of the Public Works Department and adding them to the charges made by the Auditor General for expenses of the experimental farms. The hon. gentleman has cited the Auditor General. He flas appealed unto Caesar. I agree to that appeal, and I go before Caesar with him. And Caesar, in the person of the Auditor General, tells us in his report that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) is entirely wrong. It could hardly be otherwise, because the figures that I have given with respect to the experimental farms are identically the figures of the Auditor General himself.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Mr. Fisher) and the Postmaster General (Sir William Mulock) and the other ministers are dealing with the public funds of this country. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Fisher) says to the people of this country : I have spent $84,000 of your money in running the experimental farms. I say that that statement is not correct. I go to the source of the information to which the hon. gentleman has referred me-the Auditor General's Report. I take every dollar that was paid in connection with the farms in order that I may know what the expense to the country of those farms has been. The Auditor General simply keeps accounts of the money he distributes for all purposes
Under different heads.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Of course. But, under whatever head it may appear that does not affect the amount that the people have to pay for the running these experimental farms. Could any farmer in the country run his farm without paying for fuel and light ? And why has not the hon. gentleman the manliness to charge all the amounts of such expenditure in connection with these experimental farms ? I submit that question as a practical question to any farmer in the country. The farmers of this country have put this hon. gentleman in as Minister of Agriculture, and he is supposed to handle their money carefully and with judgment. He reports to the farmers that he has spent $84,000 of their money in running the farms, but he says nothing about other items aggregating $20,000 that has beeu spent in this connection. Suppose that the president of a company or the manager of a bank were to make a statement to his shareholders in which he left out of account $20,000 of the expenses incurred in running the company, how long would he be allowed to hold his position ? Why, he would not be left in office twenty-four hours. And that is what I call upon the farmers to do, to say to this hon. gentleman : You have published a false statement of your expenditure
I give just what the Auditor General gives.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The bon. gentleman says that he appeals to the Auditor General. Well, I will meet him at the Auditor Gen-errals office at any hour to-day or to-morrow, or any day next week
Except Sunday.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Yes, except Sunday ; 1 won't work on Sunday and I won't travel on Sunday. I will meet him in the Auditor General's office at anytime he likes and will accept the Auditor General's statement as to the correctness of what I say.
I shall not go to the Auditor General

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: You are backing out already.

No, there is no need to go to the Auditor General, for he is here in this report. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) is subjecting himself to unnecessary worry. He used to be on this side of the House, and supported a former Minister of Agriculture. But he did not indict that minister because of the way the accounts were made out although they were kept in exactly the same form as before by the Auditor General and by the farm accountant. I am sorry he thinks the Auditor General makes up the accounts so badly.
Mr. TAYLOR, He has made them up correctly, and I quoted from his report.
Mr. FISHER, I have taken the figures exactly as they are in the Auditor General's Report. So the hon. gentleman need not get excited over it.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I am not excited. But I represent a constituency of farmers and I do not want them to be deceived.
This is a case, evidently, where appearances are deceitful. I am sorry the hon. gentleman should appear to be excited when he is not excited.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: It is my nature.
I think it is. And I will let it go at that, acknowledging that nature is too strong for us sometimes.

Probably we can get along without being excited, if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fisher) who has charge of this matter will be fair. The statement at page 420 of the Experimental Farm report, issued by the hon. gentleman, is headed in this way : ' Statement of Expenditure on the Experimental Farms for the Year ending June 30th. 1003.' Then the expenditure for the several farms is set out, all in the same manner. It will be sufficient for my purpose to read the heading of the first,-
' Central Experimental Farm, Expenditure 1902-3.' Now the hon. gentleman says he will appeal unto Caesar in the person of the Auditor General. We are having a great
variety of names for that gentleman of late, many of them not very complimentary, I am sorry to say. Csesar was a warrior, a great military genius, and, as we are appealing to warriors and great military men, I shall appeal to a greater military authority than even Caesar-I appeal to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fisher) himself. He can hardly object to that, for he combines the virtues of Caesar, Hannibal, Napoleon and all the rest of them. It hardly comes well from the hon. gentleman to twit the hon. member from South Leeds (Mr. Taylor) with being excited, or belligerent or anything of that kind, for, although now the hon. gentleman, while dealing with his estimates, exhibits a mild demeanour, yet. the other night upon the same question his attitude was very belligerent. He might take to himself a little of the suggestion that he has offered to the hon. member for South Leeds.
What I want to ask the hon. gentleman is this : Does it matter at all what system of book-keeping prevailed some years ago if that system is wrong V Is it fair to the country, is it fair to the farmers, whom the hon. gentleman officially represents, that he should persist in that which misleads, which deceives the people, which prevents them having an adequate grasp of the true condition of affairs ? I ask the hon. gentleman as an honest man, aye, as an honest farmer, I speak again as a farmer to a farmer, and I ask him, is he giving the people a fair representation of the case when he presents a statement Which is headed as expenditure of the farms, unless he includes in that statement all the expenditure of the farms ? Suppose the hon. gentleman is addressing a meeting in my constituency as he usually does, and some honest farmer were to say : Mr. Paterson what is the total expenditure on the experimental farm at Ottawa ? Oh, you don't believe that. in this report and no man can deny it. No man can say it is a correct statement and tell the truth. That is the whole thing in a nutshell and no one can dispute it.

It is hardly the whole thing in a nutshell. We have frequently debated in this House questions as to the system of book-keeping and for instance as to whether the distinction between capital and ordinary expenditure should not be abolished. That, however, has not been done, and the old system has been continued. I suppose the reason is that these statements are valuable for purposes of comparison. Since the farm was instituted the accountant makes up his statement on exactly the same lines, and thus you can make a comparison between the statement in 1896 and the statement in 1903. If you now added certain charges which were not added before you could not have a fair comparative statement. I am not judging the question as to whether it would not be better to change the system or not, but I am pointing out that in preserving the old system it is useful in comparing the expenditure. If you wish to adopt a new system you could not get at a comparison without adding a note to explain the difference. There is no attempt to mislead the people. The accountant does not say that it is the total expenditure, and no one can be deceived by his statement. The remedy is, easily in the hands of the Auditor General if he wishes.

speechtext: Don't obstruct the passage of the item.

The good practical common-sense farmers want to know the truth regardless of all these niceties of bookkeeping, and when the Minister of Agriculture stated in the report that the cost of the experimental farm was only $84,128.82, it was not an honest statement'of the expenses of the experimental farm. As mv friend from Leeds (Mr. Taylor) says : this is a misleading report. There is no* getting around the fact that it is not true. He said :	Who is to
blame ? I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon. I think added to that is the duty of presenting these accounts to the public.

I was going to say tliat. In regard to the accounts of the Public Works Department, it is his duty to ascertain whether the expenditure has been made in accordance with the conditions of the vote of parliament and the law which provides for such expenditure. When he finds that it is correct, he has a right to show it to the public in some way. He puts it under the various branches, and shows it by his index, and in doing that he has done his full duty. He has nothing to do with showing how or where the money has been expended on the farm ; and the Minister of Customs, instead of blaming the Auditor General, should blame the Minister of Agriculture, whose duty it is to show how and for what the expenditure has taken place. The hon. Minister of Agriculture says the hon. member for South Leeds chooses to appeal to Caesar, meaning that the Auditor General is Caesar. Well, Caesar was right and Fisher was wrong, that is the only difference. It is not the duty of the Auditor General to compile the different expenditures and to say : Everything that was spent on the farm is to be found here. He shows by his index where it is to be found under the various heads, and in doing that he has done his whole duty. On the other hand, what is the position of the Minister of Agriculture ? Suppose all these farms belonged to me, and I put a steward there to run them, and placed at his disposal so much cash for that purpose ; and suppose I instructed him to make a statement to me yearly as to what had been done on these farms. Suppose I owned a farm at Ottawa, another at Nappan, another at Brandon, another at Indian Head and another at Agassiz ; and suppose I looked over the statement he made to me to see what had been done with my money and how much it had cost to run each of these farms ; what am I to expect by that statement ?. Am I to regard it as giving part of the expenditure or the whole of it ? I put my steward over the different properties and ask him to render me an account which will show the income and expenditure on all these different farms. Would I regard him as doing his duty or as [DOT]worthy of the position he occupies if he rendered me an account which misled me ? As a farmer I .was misled by the account given in the hon. minister's report. If I ask any farmer in this country to tell me what it lias cost to run these farms, will he not take that account on page 429 of this report and say, there is the account of the expenditure. this House keep a steward who managed his farm in such a way as that ? I have been listening carefully to the discussion, and I have one suggestion to make to the hon. member for South Leeds (Mr. Taylor) The question that he refers to is one that ought to be discussed in Committee of Public Accounts. It is a question of the method of keeping accounts, and it is almost a waste of time to discuss such a question here.
At one o'clock committee took recess.
Committee resumed at Three o'clock.

I would ask the Minister of Agriculture to turn to page 78 of the report of the experimental farms. The hon. gentleman will find there under the heading ' Balance sheet or financial statement of live stock feeding operations on 200 acre farm. July 1, 1902 to June 30, 1903.' A table is given under the heading of comparative receipts. Commencing at the top of that table the number of horses is given at 19 in 1902 ; in 1903 they are at the same number. The returns are put down at $2,011.20. That return is extended in the column of gross returns made up of increase Mr. TAYLOR.
in value, value of products and animals sold. Will the hon. gentleman tell us how he arrives at that $2,041.20 ?

My hon. friend will notice that the statement is under the heading of ' Balance sheet or financial statement of live stock feeding operations on 200 acre farm, July 1, 1902 to June 30, 1903.' The whole of the horses on the farm are charged there, 19 in number. That is the return of the value of their work on the experimental farm of 200 acres, and the value of their work apart from this.

There is a statement here that does not quite accord with, the hon. gentleman's statement. It says :
In the case of horses, the services of the nineteen head are valued at $3,061.80, but since the labour of 6 horses is required to do the work on the 200-acre farm, only $2,041.20, or two-thirds of the value of their labour is credited to them.
That would mean, since there are only six horses engaged, $340 for each horse. Now how is that arrived at ? How is the work of six horses put down at that value ? Other horses are running about the fields or the barnyard. How is that enormous sum of $3140 arrived at as the value of each horse ?

I was not quite correct in what I said before, I cannot myself quite understand that statement. It appears to be contradictory. I will have, to telephone to the accountant and find out just what that means.

Perhaps the hon. gentleman can explain the next item : ' Shorthorns, pure bred and grade.' On July 1st, 1902, there were 16, valued at $2,155, or an average price of $135 each. The next year there were 20, valued at $3,410, or an average of $170 each, making a difference between the two years of $1,255 increase. Then under the heading of ' Returns ' there is $627.77, making an increase in value altogether of $1,882.77. Will the hon. gentleman tell us how that has arisen ?

In the first place, there is an increase in the number of animals. In the second place the 20 animals are different from the 16 animals. Then the animals are valued at the beginning of the year and at the end - of the year, showing th;ft they had increased in value. The increase in the value of the 20 over the value of the 16 is the amount which the hon. gentleman mentions, $1,255. Then in addition, the produce sold from these animals is put down at $627 17. Part of that produce sold is the number of calves, and part is milk production. The two things together make up the sum that is to be credited to the shorthorn herd as their product during the year ; that is to say, the increase in value of the animals and the value of the product

sold during the year, amount together to $1,882.77.

It cannot be milk, because that is charged on the other side of the account. The hon. gentleman accounts for it in this way : That in 1902 there were 16 animals, and in 1903 there were 20 animals. The average price in 1902 was $135, and the average price in 1903 was $170. Now how many of these animals that were there in 1902 were there in 1903 ; how many were purchased, and what was paid for the animals in the meantime ?

I have not under my hand a list of the animals or of the individual animals . I cannot tell how many of those 16 are included in the 20. I have a list of the cows in the-earlier part of the report, but that would not include the bulls. But the fact is there were 20 animals at the end of the year and 16 at the beginning. That not only causes an increase in value by the 4 additional head, but the probability is that some of these animals were of greater value at the end of the year than at the beginning, arising from their growth and their increased productiveness. Each animal is valued separately, and its just and fair value at the time the valuation is taken is put upon it.

The farm report gives a balance in favour of the live stock operation of $2,245.26. That includes an allowance for the feed of all kinds given to these animals, but from the figures given here it would seem that the amount paid to the men enumerated as being employed in the care of this stock came to $2,856. I notice in the Auditor General's Report that the sum put down for wages for the care of stock is $3,087.45. I am sure that the hon. gentleman will scarcely say that that is the whole cost of the raising of this stock. There are other men connected with the farm whose salaries have been paid, and the live stock should bear at least some proportion of these salaries as well as the other branches. I refer to such officials as the director, the accountant, &c.

I can only say that the statement on pages 78 and 79 of the Farm Report is a summary of the work on the 200-aere farm, which includes in its management the stock on the experimental farm. The statement was prepared in a summary form, and does not pretend to go into all details. I confess that I do not understand the situation in regard to the horses, and I have sent for that information. There are a large number of employees on the farm who have nothing to do with the stock. The charge for the care of stock in the Auditor General's Report is different from that in the Farm Report, and I do not understand the difference. I have sent for that information also. I do not think it is fair to charge the salary of the director, &c., to the # 200-acre farm.
To what would you charge it ?

To the experimental -work. A farmer running a 200-acre farm would not have a director and an accountant. The request has been made that this account should be kept in the way a farmer would run his farm.
This is under the control of the director, and there are other persons whose services are constantly required in this connection.	*

I do not think that will be a fair charge against it. If it were an ordinary farm, the man running it would correspond to the farm foreman, or the agriculturist, who is solely directing the operations.	,
Then, too, there is no charge made for pasture for these animals during the half year when they must have pasture.

I do not at the moment see anything in this report for pasture, although that should be included. If the animals are fed on the farm, the pasturage ought to be charged to them the same as the feed in the winter. I will see that it is done another year.

There is an expenditure of $7,000 for printing and distribution of bulletins and reports, which is not charged to the farm at all. Is it not an expenditure in connection with the farm, and why is it not charged to it ?

It is an expenditure in the way of distributing the knowledge acquired on the farm, but, of course, it is in no way connected with the operations of the farm. It is done by a staff of clerks who are paid specially out of this $7,000, and it appears on both sides of the balance.

Coming from an agricultural district, I may be excused for saying a word or two on this matter. The hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor) stated that he did not distribute any of the reports of the agricultural department to the people in his riding. I am not in that position, because there is no departmental report that I have distributed so freely as this one. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) stated that he did not distribute these reports because he did not wish to distribute any thing that was false. I consider myself just as honourable and as honest as he is, but I regret to say that I am not in that position, because I sent out these reports believing that they contained the truth and up to the present debate I was not aware that they are misleading. It is true that certain matters which were brought out in the discussion last year and the year before led me to believe that these agricultural reports were to some extent wrong. For instance, when I questioned the

minister as to. how he valued his hay, he said he valued it at eight dollars per ton and he weighed it as it came in from the field, whereas every one knows that hay is supposed to shrink about one-third, and the course pursued by the minister in that respect was to my mind greatly misleading. However, I did not think the report of the Agricultural Department was misleading to the extent it is. I have had many applications for these reports by my constituents in North Middlesex, and I sent them out without any explanation. It would appear now that in order to have them properly understood I should have sent the Auditor General's Report along with them. Had I sent the Auditor General's Report out at the same time as the agricultural report, I believe the farmers of North Middlesex are quite intelligent enough to go through both reports *and arrive at correct conclusions from a study of each, but placing that agricultural report in the hands of any man it is not possible for him to understand it correctly, or to see that there should be $19,000 added to the expenses of the farm more than is therein stated. I was amazed to hear the Minister of Agriculture say that this report is not misleading. To my mind that is a ridiculous statement. I was pleased with what the Minister of Customs said to some extent; because, although he tried to go all round it he did not undertake to justify the report or to say that it was not misleading. However, he did say that because the wicked Tories had done the same thing prior to 1890, that was sufficient justification for the Minister of Agriculture to send out a misleading report. I am satisfied that not one of these gentlemen on the opposite side of the House in discussing public questions on the platform has ever referred to the fact that the expenditure on the experimental farm is much larger than is shown in the report. On the contrary they based their remarks on the figures contained in it ns being found in the blue-book that could1 not lie. 1 may say that from this out, when sending lout the report of the Agricultural Department. I intend to send an explanation stating the real facts of the case. Not only is this report misleading to men who seek information, but I think it is a very bad example to the young men of our country that a man occupying the high position of Minister of Agriculture should not only send out this misleading report, but should stand up in the House as he did and state it was not misleading. I fail to see how any person of the intelligence and ability of the Minister of Agriculture could say that this Agricultural report is not misleading. It is said that the Auditor General's Reports are public property. That is true, but every one is well aware that there are a dozen of the agricultural reports put in the hands of the public for every one of the Auditor General's Reports. There is no possible way for Mr. SHERRI IT.
the average farmer to find out what the true state of affairs Is by reading that report as it is at present published. I do not wish to detain the House, but coming from an agricultural district as I do, I consider it is my duty to stand up here and confess to having sent these reports out not knowing they were misleading and that there was an additional expenditure of $19,000 in connection with that farm which was not known to the public.
Mi-. CLANCY. I notice that the teams are Put down at $2.50 a day, which of course includes the man. If you allow the man $1.25 a day that would leave another $1.25 a day for the team, and of course the horses have to be fed. Suppose the six horses worked 300 days, instead of having $2,000 to their credit they would only have $375. Then there is a charge of 21 cents a bushel for threshing. That is the ordinary price paid to these machines going around the country, but the men have to be fed in addition to that and the 21 cents a bushel does not anywhere near represent the cost. The hon. gentleman knows perfectly well that there is not a man in Canada who could get his threshing done, including the pay of the men engaged, their board and so on. for 21 cents a bushel. Every farmer in the House knows that that is perfectly ridiculous. I would like to know how that figure is arrived at.

In the first place, let me reply in regard to the horses. If the hon. gentleman will look at the bottom of page 58 and at the top of page 59, he will find a full explanation of the cost of the horses. It shows that on a team there is a margin of 32 cents a day, after paying for the feed of the horses, and $1.41$ per day for the driver. The 32 cents per day covers the wear and tear on the harness and replacing the horses as they grow old. A daily allowance of 16 cents per horse amounts to $48 in the year of 300 working days. That shows abundant margin left for wear and tear on the harness and for replacing the horses. If the hon. gentleman examines that account, I think he will find it accurate.
I cannot myself see any flaw in it.

I will point out the flaw.
In the first place, the calculation is made on nineteen horses when only six are used. When you divide the amount among nineteen, you will get a much smaller amount for each horse.

The calculation is worked out for each horse ; it does not matter whether the number is nineteen or six. When you take a pair of horses to do some work, we charge that to two horses. The cost of feeding and caring for a team comes to $2.16. We base this on 300 working days ; but when the account is for eating, the charge is for 365 days. For the cost of horse labour $2.50 per day is allowed for each .

*working day, which leaves a margin of 32 cents on a team, for wear and tear of harness and replacing horses as they grow old. That 32 cents on 300 working days amounts to $48 for every horse on the farm, which is an abundant sum to cover wear and tear of harness and the replacing'of the horses.

To what account is charged the days on which the horses are standing idle ? I will give an extreme example, and will put the average cost of a horse at just what is stated here. Suppose the horses work only one month during the year, do you simply charge their labour at the rate of $2.50 a day, and keep them for the whole year ? The kon. gentleman has kept these horses at a certain expense, and he is not charging that to any other service. The statement is entirely misleading.

I will take the hon. gentleman exactly at his word. I only wish to make a fair statement, and I take the statement shown as one. Six horses on a 200-acre farm would have to work practically 300 days in the year.	,
Do they work half that ?

Yes, as a matter of fact there are not ten days in the year in which the horses on the experimental farm are idle. I say that positively, because there is a great variety of work, and the horses are kept working all the time, every month in the year. In the winter time there is teaming to be done, hauling manure, and a great deal of teaming backwards and forwards to the city. That might not and would not be the case on an ordinary farm; but at the same time I think my hon. friend or any other farmer would arrange his work so that six horses on a 200-acre farm would be employed 300 days in the year. If he did not do that, his management of the farm would not be as economical and careful as it might be. The statement is based on a horse working 300 days in the year, which gives them about 15 days ordinary working days in which they would not do anything. The work of each team is charged at the rate of $2.50 per day, which I do not think is unreasonable. The details are given on page 59.

I do not think there is any man of experience in the use of horses in this House who will say that even in the most favourable wjeather, you can use a horse more than twenty days in a month. The hon. gentleman astounds me when he adheres to that calculation made to show that any man could employ a team of horses during 300 days in the year. If you can get a farmer in this House who will back that statement, I will make the hon. minister a public apology.

We have at the farm the actual details of what every horse does
every day, and I will incorporate a summary of that in next year's report.
The hon. gentleman would also have to incorporate a certificate as to the perfect sanity and character of the man who would make such a statement.

It is quite evident from the discussion we have had that the report of the Minister of Agriculture is completely misleading as regards the expenditures on the experimental farm. When this report of the Minister's Department is sent out, the public accept it of course as giving a correct statement of the facts; and if any one on the hustings were to declare that the experimental farm at Ottawa costs more than was set down in the report, no one would be inclined to believe him. But we have it amply proved in this debate that no less a sum than $19,000 has been left out in the statement of expenditure. That sum has been expended on the different experimental farms but not one dollar of it is accounted for in this report. Of course we can understand that the minister who not only has charge of the Department of Agriculture-the most important in the country and one which gives abundant scope for the exercise of all his energies and ability-but also at intervals takes charge of the Department of Militia, cannot be held strictly accountable, but it is high time that the people should know how this department is managed. Why should the people's money be spent in getting up a report which is absolutely incorrect ? How are we to find out how much is spent on these farms ? As the great taxpayers of this country, we have a right to have a proper report and not a partisan report. We have a right to a report that will enable us to make comparisons between the acts of this government and of their predecessors. I remember that when hon. gentlemen opposite were appealing to the country, they criticised these points of book-keeping and declared that if they were put in power they would submit the accounts to the public in such fashion that everybody might know how the money was spent. And they said : If we do not act in accordance with our professions. turn us out. The amount of money they are spending and the way they are accounting for it is a flat contradiction of every promise which they gave in this respect, and I believe that at the next appeal the country will take them at their word and turn them out. I hope that in the future we shall not have such a wrangle about these points but that the facts will be placed before the people so fairly and so clearly that there will be no difficulty in understanding what is the actual cost of these experimental farms.

I would like to call attention to page 59 of the Experimental Farm Reports. It shows that for the twelve

months from December 1st, 1902, to November 30th, 1903, the food of the horses was valued at $1,552.10. To care for the horses cost $560, making a total cost of $2,112.10 for 19 head, or $111.16 to feed and care for one horse for the year, or 37 cents per day, counting 300 working days in the year. Now, why confine it to the 300 working days of the year ? These horses had to be kept for the 365 days of the year.
Mi-. FISHER, The total cost of keeping each horse is $111.16, and if this were aver aged over 365 days it would make less than 37 cents per day. This would cause a reduction in the apparent cost for each working day. If we were to do that, the hon. gentleman would have a right to complain that we did not provide for the keep of the horses for those days when they were not working. We have charged up against the 300 working days enough to cover the cost of the keep of the horses for the 365 days of the year.
The statement of the hon. minister is, perhaps, correct. If so, I was in error

I am sure my statement is the true explanation, and that the hon. gentleman's criticism was 'based upon a misapprehension. I would like to say to him also that I have an explanation about the comparative statement with regard to the horses (page 78), to which he referred. I have not seen the officer who is in charge of this department, but I can see through it now in a way I could not before. It says :
In the ease of horses, the services of the nineteen head are valued at $3,061.80, but since the labour of six horses is required to do the work on the 200-acre farm, only $2,041.20, or two-thirds of the value of their labour is credited to them.
The reason for that is this: The feed raised by the 200-acre farm feeds all the horses and the rest of the live stock on the farm that we are now taking account of. But the work of six of these horses is required for the 200-acre farm. Therefore, we have no right to credit all the 19 horses with doing work. But if we have 13 horses whose work is not applied to the 200-acre farm, but is given to the rest of the experimental farm establishment, then the 200-acre farm deserves to be credited with the value of the services of these 13 horses. For all practical purposes it is enough if one-third of the value of the services of all the horses is left out, because about one-third of the labour of all is applied to the 200-acre farm and two-thirds is applied to the other work in the experimental farm establishment.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Fisher) has pointed out that only six horses are doing the work. Are not the other 13 also working horses ?

Not all engaged in farm work. There is the horse that draws the 1 Mr. CLANCY.
'bus to and from the farm, and the horse used for driving purposes. They have nothing to do with the 200-acre farm.
Then why should they be taken into account in the way of profit ?
Because the 200-acre farm feeds and provides for them.
But he is giving credit of $2,041 to six horses that are working.

The six horses are necessary on the 200-acre farm, and their services are not counted. Their maintenance has to be provided by the 200-aere farm, and therefore they are not charged with their maintenance or credited with their work. But this 200-acre farm also supports 13 other horses, whose work is not necessary on the 200-acre farm. They might be kept elsewhere and put at outside work and, if they were, the 200-acre farm would have a right to be credited with the value of their services.
But they are not performing any.

They are performing services for the rest of the establishment. The other parts of the establishment are benefiting by these horses that are maintained on the 200-aere farm. Suppose that the 200-acre farm raised 1,000 bushels of oats and that Dr. Saunders, as director, took the oats and sent them out to farmers all over the country, would it not be fair to credit the 200-acre farm with the 1,000 bushels of oats? You certainly ought to, just the same as if they were taken to the market and sold. So the hay, the oats, the meal and the work of the men are charged to the 200-acre fai-m, and are applied to the keep of the 13 horses which are not needed for the work on that farm. Therefore, we credit this item with two-thirds of the keep of 19 horses, only one-third of the 19 horses being needed for the farm, and we credit the farm with two-thirds of the keep of the horses which are not used.
The hon. gentleman states that only 6 horses are employed on the 200 acre farm.
The 13 horses are working for somebody else.

Here are 6 horses employed. If you have ten men and only employ five, you are certainly not going to pay wages to those you do not employ.
Mr. FISHER, These horses are working elsewhere, but they are fed and maintained there on the farm. Supposing the hon. member was a farmer and he required for his own use 4 horses. But he had an opportunity in the neighbourhood of running some teams for a lumber yard or a brick yard, and he kept on his farm 16 other horses and he fed them there, and fed the men and

maintained them there. But if he got his wages for sending them out to work for others, would he not consider it right to credit his farm with so much of the wages that he got for letting out those horses V This is a similar instance. The 200 acre farm requires 6 horses, but it maintains and feeds 13 other horses which are used on another part of the experimental farm, and that other part must pay to the 200 acre farm the value of the services of those horses, and this item is the value of the services-of those horses which is credited to the 200 acre farm.

Assuming the horses were of the same value, although only 0 of them worked out of the 19, it would mean the live stock were entitled to a credit of $2,041. On the other side of the account, the feed of course is charged up for the keep of the 19 horses. But there is no statement here showing how that $2,041 is arrived at.
The paragraph above is not quite so clear as it might be. I did not understand it when I first read it.
The hon. gentleman will see that each horse has to earn over $100, each one of the 19, because they are credited with $2,041.

I have just been given a list of the work done by the other horses. There are 3 for the omnibus, 4 are used for the Horticultural Department, 3 or 4 keep the lawns in order, and 3 are riders. This makes up the 13 horses extra.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: And there are 13 men to look after them ?
The men who look after the horses go with them. But I think my hon. friend understands now the explanation which I have given.
I will understand if the hon. gentleman tells me how he arrives at what each horse earns, and how he earns it.
The services of the horses are put down at $3,061.80.

How is that arrived at ?
Mi". FISHER. I will have that worked out in a minute or two. Perhaps there are some other questions the hon. gentleman would like to ask me in the meantime.
I may say that I do not intend to prolong the debate. I only want to see how he arrives at that figure.
I would like to know that myself. I take the figures from my officers as being correct, and I have no doubt they are. I have found, when I tested them by working them out, that they were correct.

In working them out, it might be well to make this further calculation. I am unable to understand why we should take six horses and credit two thirds
of the value of their labour to them, as in the statement on page 78 of the report.
The word 'their' in that statement on page 78 is improperly used. It refers not to the work of the six horses but of the nineteen horses.
I would ask the minister what position Mr. W. S. Sparks occupies in the department and what his salary is.
He is not now in the department nor in this country, but during the last winter he was employed for some institute work.
At whose request was he employed in the institute work ?

He was introduced to me and in conversation discussed matters connected with horse breeding and training in this country. He had been recommended to me by a number of people and he asked me if he could not perform any service for the department. I then put him on to give addresses on horse training, &c., and he also acted as judge at various shows with the approval of the department.
Was he employed permanently ?
No ; he received so much a day and expenses in the usual way.

I feel interested in these estimates because I am interested in agriculture. Every member in this House, no matter whether he is a practical farmer or a lawyer, is interested in agriculture simply because one half of all the exports of this country are the products of agriculture. Therefore anything that could be done to encourage.farming and to induce the farmer to produce more productions of a better quality is of great good to our country. I think the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor) is entitled to the thanks of the country for having elicited a good deal of information in reference to the false system of book-keeping that has been practised ever since confederation, apparently, in regard to the experimental farm. I hope that from this time forward the Minister of Agriculture will see that everything in connection with the farms is so placed that there will be nothing misleading about it and that every man reading the returns will be able to tell exactly how much the experimental farm costs us. The minister says that this system was inaugurated long before he, became minister and therefore he claims that he is not responsible for it, but he knew about it and_when he knew about it, he should have amended it. Therefore the minister will pardon me if I say that he should not be excused and cannot blame the hon. member for Leeds for bringing this matter up because it certainly is, as the hon. member for East Middlesex (Mr. Gil-mour) says, misleading. Yesterday we had

an agricultural discussion and I suppose it would be hardly proper for me to refer to it, but I may say that I voted against the minister yesterday afternoon simply because I considered that he had not discharged his duty in the matter of placing an official weigher in Montreal. That thing has been discussed and the matter settled, and I hope that the minister will see that the farmers of the country get justice, so that when they send their stuff to market there will be some one there with authority to stand between the buyer and seller and see that justice is done. This matter seems so far to have been neglected but I hope that the resolution will not be in vain. Every farmer on that side should have voted for it yesterday, and they would have done so if they had heard the question discussed but many of them were not in the House. I do not wish to make any further remarks on this subject but I would say that I am prepared to assist the Minister of Agriculture in everything that he can do to aid the farmers. Complaints have been made in reference to the cold storage systems that have been started in different parts of the Dominion. I think that this cold storage is all right and that inducements should be offered to start cold storage plants all over this country. Tuere is no doubt but that ultimately they will be established in every city, town and village because they are a necessity and because they will enhance the value of all our perishable products. Therefore I think the minister is right when he encourages the farmers to make use of this system. I would like to send reports of the experimental farms to all the farmers in my riding, but I do not think I had better send them out unless there is a foot note to the effect that all the lighting and all the coal is charged to the Public Works Department. I think a farmer would make a very poor showing if he did not take into calculation the cost of fuel, wood, &c., on his farm. I think he would soon come out at the wrong end, because it is a matter of great importance, and $19,000 is about one-fifth of the cost of the whole experimental farm. Thus one-fifth of the real cost of running this experimental farm is charged to capital account or some other account. X hope that in the future this will all be set forth so plainly that he who runs may read.
I do not believe it is possible for each horse to work 300 days in the year, but at all events we are dealing with the live stock section here and not with a 200 acre farm.
I think there is some-tiling in the argument of my hon. friend but as the work of six horses was requited for that 200 acre farm we credit their services to it.
In order to be consistent, the minister should revise these figures. Evidently he has mixed up the farm with the live stock.
How many thoroughbred cattle are on the farm, and to what breeds do they belong ?
The statement on page 78 shows the breeds but does not say how many are pure and how many grade.
You have them mixed up. How do you make the returns ?
These returns are the revenue from the animals and their increase in value ; if they decrease in value it would be deducted.
What do you /do with the swine ?
We breed them and sell them. The chief revenue is from young pigs for breeding purposes and the sale of fat pigs raised on experimental work to the butcher.
Are the pigs all pure bred ?

Not all, but most of them.
Patent Record, $5,000.

This is an additional vote, caused by the increased numbers of patents issued. It is all for printing, and is paid over to the Printing Bureau. We get a larger revenue, of course.
Experimental farms, $10,000.

This is to cover last year's expenditure, which is brought up )to the amount I ask for this year.
Exhibitions, $45,000.
Does this include the St. Louis exhibition ?
Yes.
Whom have you sent as commissioner to that exhibition ?
Mr. William Hutchison is the only commissioner.
What other officers are there ?

There are a number of secondary officers, men in charge, besides certain officers who have been sent to explain our exhibits. I will get a list of them for the hon. gentleman, and in the meantime we can let the item stand.
Item allowed to stand.
For the branch of the Commissioner of Agriculture and Dairying, including live stock, dairy, cold storage, extension of markets, poultry, seed and fruit division ; employees paid from this sum not to be subject to the Civil Service Act, $220,000.

This is the usual item for this branch of my department. It is the same amount as we have had for the year just past. Some expenditures which we have had during the last year will not be needed in the future, because the payments for cold storage on steamship lines are closed up, and we shall not have to spend the same amount for that service this year that we did last year ; but I propose to extend the service in other directions, so that we shall require about the same amount of money.
Mi'. SPROULE. What work is being carried on under this branch ?
Mr. FISHER, In the first place, we have work of a general character in regard to the commerce and transportation of agricultural products. The branch is divided into seven main divisions, which are set out in the report of the department for the year. I wTill give the estimated expenditures for the ensuing year :
General head office	$31,000
Live stock division	 34,000
Dairy division	 61,000
Cold storage division	 19,600
Fruit division	 25,500
Seed division	 17,900
