How many hands employed in the general head offices ?
Mr. FISHER, Besides the commissioner, whose salary is $5,000, there are employed Mr. O'Hara, Mrs. Henderson, Mr. Thomas, and several others and the messengers, whose aggregate salaries amount to $5,650. Then there is the publishing work, for which the clerical staff costs $1,500. There are also the renting of offices, $1,800 ; caretaker, $500 : messenger, $365 ; printing and stationery, $3,500 ; travelling expenses, $1,800 ; and contingencies, $4,400. About $4,500 are left open to be allocated according to any plan that may be worked out during the year requiring extra expenditure.
What are you doing in the live stock line ?

We provide lectures and assistance to various fat stock shows. My hon. friend no doubt attended the Guelph fat stock show and must have noticed the great interest taken there in the department where illustrations, demonstrations and lectures were delivered. The interest taken in these is simply wonderful and that is the work to which we specially devote ourselves.
How much do you pay for these lectures ?
I propose next year to devote about $4,000 to the five shows.
Then you have $30,000 left.

There have been established what are called straight stallion shows and breeding animal shows at different points. For these we have laid aside STOOD. We have undertaken work in connection with the ordinary fairs-the country and township local fairs. We have been trying to get those established on a fixed basis, so as to have a certain amount of similarity in the prize list and management. We hope to make these fairs model fairs. Our work in the Whitby fair was very. flatteringly commented on.
Does the hon. gentleman's department co-operate with the local directors ?

Yes, these fairs are entirely managed by their local associations. We only advise" them when they write and ask us. The live stock commissioner has had many experiences in that work when em-ploved by the Ontario government as institute manager. That is, when they ask for a little help in this respect we give it. We have not been giving them any prizes or any money for them to spend ; but when they come and say that in this or that respect they are a little weak, we try, by sending them a judge or some one to help them in their management, to improve the quality, management and style of these fairs. We set aside $1,000 for this purpose.
Upon what principle do you divide it ? Does the minister give assistance to every one who applies ?

A thousand dollars would not go far if we did that. We try to make conditions that we will give aid when the -people do certain things. Speaking. from memory the only fairs that have received assistance of this kind so far are those of Whitby and Richmond, Ontario.
This accounts for about $6,000 out of a vote of $34,000. What is the balance to be devoted to ?

A part will be devoted to work in connection with auction sales of live stock in British Columbia, tbe Northwest Territories, Ontario and the maritime provinces. The live stock associations ot these provinces have been arranging for auction sales of live stock, and we have been helping in the work. That will cost us according to our present plans $2,450. Then we have been helping local fairs with expert judges. Some years ago there was a good deal of dissatisfaction expressed as to the men obtainable as judges for small local fairs. The suggestion was made that we should try and supply competent men to judge the various classes exhibited. We have been able, by arrangement with well known judges of different classes of live stock, to secure their services. In response to the applications sent us from the local fairs, we have been able to supply a very considerable number of expert judges, sometimes officers of the departments and sometimes men whom we have secured from outside. We have had most appreciative letters from the different fairs where these gentlemen have acted, and the demand for their services is growing all the time. We have now hundreds of requests from all over the country to send judges of this or that class of live stock to the different fairs.
What do you pay these judges?

We pay them $3 a day and their travelling expenses. We do not pay for their maintenance at the place where the fair is held, but make it a rule that the people shall entertain them. We seek to arrange a circuit for each man so as to reduce the expense.
Are only Grits employed on this job ?

Not at all. I could give a long list of men thus employed who are strong supporters of the opposition. I do not say there are no Grits, because, as the hon. gentleman knows, many of the best live stock men in Canada are Grits. But I might mention, for instance, Mr. Joseph Brethour who is one of the leading swine breeders of the country and who has always been* a good Conservative. We have employed him for the last two or three years. Another name that occurs to me is Robert Johnston, of South Ontario, who never cast a Grit vote in his life, I believe.
. Mr. SPROULE. How much of this vote will be used in this service 1

About $3,700. One feature introduced with regard to the work of these judges has proven very acceptable. We have asked the judges to explain their reasons for their judgment, illustrating their talk with the animals in the ring. In this Mr. SPROULE.
way they point out exactly why one animal was given first prize, another second prize and another none. Under the old practice, the judge made the award and nobody knew why-sometimes the audience found it pretty hard to understand. But we have insisted that our judges give reasons for their opinions. I have been told by many farmers personally that it Is a grand thing to give the public in this way the opinions of competent judges.

When a man is sent out to judge, let us say, horses, at a fair, does he become the absolute judge of that department V Are the prizes awarded on his statement alone, or does he co-operate with the local judges ?
The one-judge system at fairs is being more generally adopted. Our judges generally act alone. But, of course, we only send them out on request.
Are we to understand that where a board of directors send in word that they require the services of a judge the minister will send out a competent man at the' expense of the department ?
WTe have been doing a great deal of that, making no charge ex-,cept that we require that the people shall entertain the judges.
That is not quite what I wanted to know. Suppose that twenty counties ask for a judge, will the minister send a judge to each of them ?
Wherever we can. But if we are not able to get competent judges if we will not send out anybody in whom we have not the most perfect confidence.
Will the minister send to the same place repeatedly ? For instance, I understand that some judges were sent to Whitby last year ; will he send judges every year to the same place ?
I think so. We sent to thirty-three fairs last year altogether.
What other lines does the minister intend to take up that will require the balance of this item ?	.

We have been doing a good deal in the way of institute lectures. The local governments, as a general rule, carry on institute work within the several provinces, They are constantly applying to us for assistance. The province of Ontario is very well equipped in that respect, but the other provinces have difficulty in getting competent men to act as lecturers. My department has a number of officers in its employ whom we are able to spare for this service during part of the year. In New Brunswick as a rule, the institutes meet for three or four weeks at one period of the year and then for three or four weeks

at another season. We try if possible to provide speakers on such and such a subject who will go round to the various constituencies, and we have been able to supply a certain number of men to meet all demands. If we can secure thoroughly competent men to do that work we are glad to do so. When an official of the department is sent out on that business his expenses are charged to this item in the estimates. We cover all the provinces to a certain extent, but we do less in Ontario, because the local government is attending to that.
What consideration do you allow them ?

Three dollars a day and their expenses. That is the price the Ontario government pays. When they are doing this work they are not paid their salary in addition. If their salary is by the year, they do not get the $3 a day, they get nothing but their expenses. We have men employed who are not on salary, but who engage in this business for one or two months in the winter or in the summer. These get $3 a day and expenses. But when a man is an officer of the department on a salary, he gets nothing extra.
Will the hon. gentleman give us a list of all those men employed last year and bring down the amount that each got ?
I will lay that on the table.
How much have you for that ?

We take $3,575. Twenty-eight speakers were employed last year, who attended 199 meetings. Generally two of them go together, in some cases three, and in some cases one. Then we had last winter a national stock convention of live stock men who came here on invitation of the farm, to organize a live stock association somewhat on the lines of an organization of a similar character in the United States and of one in Great Britain. We hope to continue that effort, and the department will incur some expense. There is the printing of a report for distribution, stenographic expenses, and expenses in bringing people from a distance, officials who are chosen, by the local associations.
Then we are working out what is called a standard of excellence, with a bulletin or report of the work and conclusions of the live stock association. We expect that to cost $2,500. The officers of the department and the leading breeders of the country are trying to establish what we might call a score, by means of score cards, or standard of the different breeds of animals in the country, which we call a standard of excellence. We have a large number of breeds of animals, and the judges at fairs
find that the types which breeders have to aim at in their breeding are not well described. There is hardly any description of it, and the live stock commissioner with some assistance in the department is working to establish and to get out a book of standard excellence for the different breeds.
It is rather an elaborate piece of work and a difficult one. It has to be done in conjunction with the leading breeders of each particular breed. Some bulletins will be issued in connection with that work. We Shall have to spend money in the way of getting information, and employing a clerk to compile it. Then we will have to pay for printing and issuing that information There are a great many cuts and illustrations of the typical animals of each breed which will be included, and these will be expensive. Then bulletins on the subject will be issued and will have to be paid for, as well as the printing and distribution.
Then there is work in connection with a national live stock record. My hon. friend will remember that the meeting of the live stock men this winter asked us to establish a Dominion record. That is a pretty difficult task. There are local records to-day in different parts of the country. We wish to carry out the views and ideas of the live stock men of that convention, and I think their aim is a very laudable one. The object is to have one thoroughly recognized record for every particular breed in this country. At the present time there are records in Quebec, Nova Scotia, Ontario and in the west, but one does not recognize the other in every case. The consequence is that a man may buy an animal to-day which he is told is a thoroughbred, which is registered, and he may be given a pedigree and certificate of registration. But when he comes to sell that animal to somebody else, the buyer looks up some other record to find the animal, and he does not find it, and he says this animal is not a pure bred. Of course there is a lot of dispute and difficulty in consequence. Farmers are wasting their money and are being deceived, not intentionally perhaps, but at the same time are being deceived in the purchase of pedigree live stock. The live stock men ask us to work toward the establishment of a national record. It will be a difficult task, a great many different and sometimes conflicting interests will have to be reconciled. At the same time I want to try and bring it about, and that will involve some expenditure of money. We shall need to bring people together from different parts of the country to discuss the matter.
Then there is the suggestion of a live stock census-quite a different thing from the census we have heard so much about. There is being an effort made to improve the quality of particular dairy cows. One of the most effective pieces of work ever done, I think, in the improvement of dairy animals

has been done .by ex-Governor Hoard of Wisconsin, a well known dairy writer and authority of the United States. Governor Hoard edits and publishes a journal known as ' Hoard's Dairyman,' in the neighbourhood of his own home, where he has not only a printing office but a record office. He has been making records of the different herds of animals, and of individual animals, and showing the difference there is between the herds in different parts of the country.
The records which he has already collected are very startling and have attracted a great deal of attention in tlxe dairy world. I venture to say that no work could be done which would do so much to improve our dairy animals as the keeping of records to show the great difference of production and of work, if I may call it so, of our dairy cows. I want to inaugurate that kind of work and to try to bring it about that our dairy interests throughout the country will not only study as to which is the best herd, but as to which of the animals in each herd is doing good work and which is running her owner into debt, for X am sorry to say that there are a great many cows in this country which are not only of no use to their owners but are worse than useless because they run them into debt. A great deal of work of this kind has been done in Denmark where the dairy interests are the best organized of any in the world. I have had a report upon the system established there for this purpose and it seems to have worked out most satisfactorily. If we can accomplish one-tenth, I might almost say one-hundredth, of the good results which have been accomplished by this method in Denmark in Canada during the next ten years, we will add $1,000,000 per annum to the value of the product of the same number of cows.
Would the minister explain the superiority of the Danish over the Canadian system ?

The organization there is very superior. They have been doing work among their farmers which wo have not yet been able to accomplish. The dairymen have formed among themselves associations for this kind of work and they keep records of each cow and then compare notes. [DOT] Each association employs an expert to make tests of the milk, for butter-fat, &c. They have also adopted more generally than any other country in the world the co-operation system in dairying by which the factories are owned and operated by joint stock companies, the shares of which are held by the men who supply the milk. In that way each and every one is interested personally in his own success and in their joint success, with the result that the work is carried on in a better manner and with better organization than in any other place in the world.
What kind of cows do they use ?
Chiefly the dairy breed which is native to Denmark, called, I think, the Anglian.
Carried.
No it will not be carried for four hours unless we get the information.
Certainly the hon. gentleman will get all the information he desires.
Carried.
We come next to the dairying.
We have for dairying
To what extent have cheese makers availed themselves of these cheese curing rooms ?

We have the four establishments and they have been filled to overflowing with the exception of that at St. Hyacinthe. Those at Cowansville, Rrock-ville and Woodstock were full to overflowing all season and this year that at St. Hyacinthe is also full.
Is there any charge for the use of the rooms ?

We have taken a certain amount of the profit. There are two profits due to the curing of cheese in this room. The cheese is of a better quality so that there is an average increase in price of about one-eighth of a cent a pound. There is also less shrinkage in cheese cured in these cool curing rooms than in the ordinary curing rooms and we have taken for ourselves the difference in the shrinkage.
Do cheese shrink at all if properly cooled ? I wonder what my hon. friend from Perth (Mr. MacLaren) says to that ?

I was going to ask the minister about the paraffining of cheese. Cheese which has been paraffined does not shrink, but cheese which has not been paraffined does shrink. I have known cheese which has not been paraffined to shrink from one to three pounds a box in ordinary cellars or curing rooms in two or three months, but if the cheese is paraffined there is very little shrinkage. I would like to have the minister's opinion as to that.

The cheese in our curing rooms are not paraffined until they are about ten days old. We experimented with paraffining cheese at the very commencement, but now we wait until it is ten days old. As we know, the cheese does shrink in the first ten days of the curing, but after they are paraffined they do not shrink much more.
Do you still paraffine cheese as you put them in storage, when they are ten days old ?
Yes.
Do you think it is a good idea ?
My expert officers think so.

It would be a great mistake to paraffine them too soon and before a certain amount of evaporation takes place. It would not be a bad idea to issue to the cheese-makers throughout the country instructions as to paraffining, because sometimes they paraffine them too soon, and sometimes when they are too old.
Mr. FISHER, That information has been given.
Mr. SPROUiLE. Is it the intention to extend these four central stations 1
Mr. FISHER, These were established as a test in the curing of cheese, and also as a test of the feasibility of collecting cheese for curing under one roof. These four establishments were quite sufficient to carry out this test. I do not think it will be necessary for the government to increase the number of these curing rooms, but this year I intend to undertake the work along somewhat different lines. A good many people think that the system of central curing rooms is not so economical and efficient on the whole as to induce a large number of factories to improve their own curing rooms. I have been arranging this year to fit up and improve four ordinary cheese factories where the cheese would be cured under ordinary conditions, except that there would be the addition of a room where the temperature could be controlled. I propose to spend a little money on that.
How much ?
Where are these factories to be located ?

In the Lake St. John district. In that district the dairying is making great strides, but still they are not in a central district where they can get the advantage of these curing rooms, and we intend to fit up four factories there to illustrate this kind of work.

speechtext: Lake St. John district this year, and I find that last year $3,475 were paid as bonuses in Quebec, that Prince Edward Island got $150, and that Ontario got $325.
For what ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I believe that any factory that puts in a load of sawdust and a few loads of ice gets a bonus.

These are all butter factories ; not cheese factories.
Mr. TAYiLOR. If instead of spending $82,000 on these illustration stations he would give it in bonuses to factories producing a certain quantity, he would have object lessons all over the country, and not have the thing confined to four places all over the Dominion.

These bonuses are under a system which has been established for seven years. A bonus of $100 is paid to any butter factory which would establish a cold storage room, and this has induced factories to put in cool storage rooms and has contributed very materially to the improved quality of our butter. I believe that nearly three-fourths of all the butter factories In Canada have adopted this system. There are a great many more butter factories in Quebec than in Ontario. Every one knows that while Ontario is the great cheese-producing province, Quebec is the great butter producing province. The people of Quebec, with their natural enterprise, put up these butter factories first and got the bonuses. A great many of these factories were drawing bonuses before, but a good many did not begin until last year.
Do you give a bonus "wherever there is a butter factory ?

We give a bonus wherever there is a butter factory fitted up with cold storage and otherwise equipped in accordance with the requirements. We give $50 in the first year, and $25 in each of the two succeeding years, if it is operated, making $100 in ttuee years. I am glad to know that over two-thirds of all the butter factories in Canada have earned the bonus, the result being that during the last year or two we have not expended quite #- much as we did a few years ago. The province of Quebec is increasing its number of factories, and consequently its production of butter very largely and rapidly, and therefore draws more of these bonuses than other parts of the country- All other parts of the -country, however, are free to draw it wherever the conditions are fulfilled. My hon. friend spoke about the paraffining of cheese.
I am free to admit that there has been a difference of opinion on that subject. When paraffined cheese was first sent to England the trade viewed it with some suspicion, and in some instances sent out instructions to buyers not to buy it. But we have this noteworthy fact, that during the present * Mr. TAYLOR.
season at every one of these stations the cheese in the cool-curing rooms has been all paraffined, and this cheese has been sold under a special brand and at a higher price than any other cheese in the neighbourhood.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Mr. Evertts contradicts that.

I cannot help that ; the facts contradict Mr. Evertts. My hon. friend knows perfectly well that cool-cured cheese is sold in a class by itself and commands from one-eighth to one-quarter cent per pound more than any other cheese sold on the same board. Mr. Evertts is a well-known dairyman, and if he said that at all, he must have said it over a year ago.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: It was less than a year ago. It was last fall.

That was when the prejudice still existed with regard to paraffined cheese. I admit that when the cheese was paraffined at a day old, the results were not as good as they are to-day, when it is paraffined at ten days old.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Mr. Evertts did not refer to the paraffining at all. It was the coolcuring he referred to.

I thought the hon. gentleman said that statement had reference to the paraffining. 1 can only say that the price obtained to-day for cheese which comes out of the cool-curing rooms is sufficient to refute that statement, whether it applies to paraffining or cool-curing.
Do you pay all the cost of this system ?
Yes. When we first established these factories, nobody knew what it would cost, and we thought it advisable to facilitate as much as we could the dairymen sending their cheese to them.
Do you continue that system now ?
I do not think the hon. gentleman need assign that motive.

MacLAItEN. When cheese is properly cured, put into cold storage at the Sproper age, and properly, paraffined, its quality is greatly improved. The great difficulty is the lack of education on the part of those dealing with the cheese when to paraffine it. Last year a great many cheeses were paraffined too green and put into the cold storage room too green ; but now they are doing better and getting a higher price for the cheese. It is all a matter of education, and when that is accomplished the paraffining and cold storage of cheese will be of great benefit to the people of this country.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
Speaking of the cool curing stations, Mr. Evertts, said :
The money used in the erection and carrying on of these curing rooms was a useless expenditure. Mr. Evertts claimed that the results achieved did not warrant their continuance in operation. They did not aid the patrons in obtaining one-sixteenth of a cent more for their cheese than others.

Yes, this year.
Mr. TAYLOR, (reading)

He challenged a single person to contradict him. These rooms were held up as models for others to follow. How many had built curing rooms after the fashion of the Brock-ville pine monument ? Not a one. And as to the cost of construction, operation, &c., the country was yet in darkness, notwithstanding a deliberate promise made by Professor Rud-dick last year to give such information. Mr. Evertts said the dairymen were getting their eyes opened. .There was too much playing to the gallery by men in high places.
If anybody gets the benefit, it is the buyer, because the seller does not put his cheese Into these curing rooms. No farmer or manufacturer will hold his cheese two or three weeks. He sells to the buyers every week, and if any one puts the cheese in to thesei cool curing rooms, it must be the buyer. Take the Brockville board and you will see that the cheeses sold there have'not been in the cold storage rooms. The department paid $1,111.06 for hauling cheese to the station and deliberately bought a lot and put it in these rooms and are still holding it. They have not sold it yet, if the return brought down is correct.

I have not got this week's sales at Brockville, but I have the report of the 27th of June and I find that the prices then were eight cents, but that the cool cured cheese brought 8 3-16, 8J. 81, 8J and 81.
Who got the benefit ?

The patrbns and the bankers did. The buyer will get another benefit because when he sells in England
he will get I of a cent more or 1 of a cent more for this cool cured cheese than for the other. What is more, those paraffine cheeses that came from the cool curing room weighed more per hundred pounds of the milk put into them than did the other cheese which was sold for eight cents. So that the patrons who had their cheese in the cool room gets the advantage both ways. My hon. friend has said that no one has taken advantage of this. Why, right in Mr. Evertt's own district, I have a list of the factories who have cool curing rooms on the model of the one at Brockville, but of course not on the same scale. There are these cool curing rooms at Oxford Mills, Patterson's Corners, the Farmer's Own Factory, the Enterprise Factory and a number of others. And there is a factory with these cool rooms in the Smith's Falls section, so that the hon. gentleman will see that these factories have taken example of the model we have set them and are doing the work themselves. The object is to improve the dairy business, and we have to expend money for the purpose of getting at the facts. Then we can give the facts and data to the public and the public can make use of them. The results are not to be estimated by the returns of any individual outlay, but by the advantage which the whole industry reaps from the expenditure. That is the principle we go on in our agricultural investigations.
Is it not a fact that the minister has purchased cheese which he has not yet sold ?

When we were making the experiment we tried to put in one or two cheese in each ease from the same vat

two of them in the cool curing room and two of them in an ordinary curing room. As those cheese belonged to the patrons, it would not be fair to experiment with them at the expense of the experimenters. Therefore we bought them, and as last year the cheese market was rather demoralized, a good many we bought early in the season could not sell to advantage.
I thought that last year was a great cheese market.

If the hon. gentleman will ask the buyers and sellers he will find it was not. The patrons got high prices, but we were buyers and were in the same position as many who bought cheese at prices in the early part of the season which it has never reached since.
How much was the aggregate loss 1
The year before there was a profit and last year there was a loss. The whole transaction is not yet finished, but the loss will be under $2,000.

Does the minister know how much of that is due to the bad system

of keeping and curing cheese and how much to the fall in the market ?
There was no bad system of keeping and curing. The cheese that was cured sold at a higher price than the other.
If you paid the average price this spring, there would be necessarily a loss of two or three cents a pound after paying interest and storage.

They have been shipped to England, but we have not yet got the returns. We had to keep them for experimental purposes in order to judge of the effects of cool-curing as against the ordinary curing. Had we shoved them off on the market, we would not have been able to test them.
I thought that by the fall the cheese were pretty well sold off.

Not so soon as that. In any case it would not do to shove these cheese off on the! market a few days after they were bought.
Mr. SI'ROULE. But the hon. gentleman says he got them from week to week commencing last May. Surely they did not need to be kept until this May.
Mr. FISHER, I am told that they were sold at an average Of three or four months old. But we cannot make up a statement of the exact details until we get the returns from England.
And the hon. gentleman lost about $2,000 on the transaction ?

About that.
Mi-. SPROULE. That is an admirable example to set the farmers.

Even if we had bought these cheese as an ordinary commercial transaction we might have lost on them, as business men have lost this year. But, we had to keep the cheese regardless of the condition of the market in order to carry on the test we were making. Had we shoved them on the market to take advantage of a temporary rise in price, we might better never have bought them at all, because our tests would not have been carried out and our report could not have been made.

That is about on a par with the explanation given by the boy as to why the rabbit climbed the hemlock tree-he had to climb it, the dog was so close behind him.
Mr. TAYLOR, I find that in 1902-3, the minister purchased for the Woodstock coolcuring room, $3,085 worth of cheese, and in 1903-4, $6,829 worth. Now, can he tell us why he wanted to buy about $10,000 worth of cheese ? And will he say, in view of these purchases, that he has not been speculating in cheese ? I have the reports Mr. SPROULE.
for the other cool-curing rooms here, and I find that altogether he bought about $40,000 or $50,000 worth of cheese. The cheese that he bought for Cowansville in 1902-3 he sold at a loss of $224.78. For the next year he bought $4,103.47 worth, from which he has a revenue of $1,370. But in this return he says that the cheese for that year is not all disposed of and so the revenue is not all in.

I was asking the minister before six o'clock about the salary of the assistant to the commissioner, at St. Louis, Mr. E. P. Eastman.
Mr. FISHER, Mr. Eastman receives $7 a day to cover everything. He also receives his transportation from his home to St. Louis and back at the close of the exhibition. That is what I pay to all of those of that status.
Is the minister aware that he is not a British subject ?
No, I was not aware of that.

Mr. Eastman is not a British subject, he is an American. He has been resident for some years in New Brunswick but has always refused to become a naturalized British subject and remains an American citizen to this day. I think the minister could not have been aware of that.
Mr. FISHER, No I was not.

I suppose the minister will follow up the course which I believe is being adopted with respect to American engineers on the Grand Trunk Pacific and will at once have the appointment cancelled. It seems to me there would be enough Canadian applicants for a position of that kind and that it should be given to a Canadian rather than to a foreign citizen.
I certainly intended to appoint Canadians and I will inquire into that matter.
If the minister finds that this person is an American citizen I would like to know what course he will take.

I would like to inquire into all the circumstances of the case before making a definite answer, but cer-

tainly my policy would be to employ Canadians under all circumstances.

I can scarcely conceive of any circumstance which would justify an appointment of this kind. The fact' that this gentleman has resided for some time within the borders of Canada would not be a justification, if the gentleman has persistently refused to become a Canadian citizen. His appointment would be worse under these circumstances than if he had been on this side only a few months and had not gained that knowledge which would convince him of the superiority of Canadian over American citizenship. I would like to have a straight expression of opinion from the minister as to what he would do if the facts bear out my statement.

If the hon. gentleman's statement is absolutely accurate all through it would appear to be an exaggerated case.
I can, however imagine that a man might reside in this country for many years and not become naturalized. In my own county which is a border district I have known men to live in Canada for 20 or 30 years who have never gone through the form of naturalization, and the question of their citizenship has never come up unless they have sought to vote at an election and have been challenged. Of course if my hon. friend is correct in saying. this gentleman has persistently refused in an offensive way to become a Canadian citizen that would have to be taken into consideration. I would not care to say more than I have, that in a general way my policy would be to employ Canadians only, and if an individual in the government employ showed himself to be antagonistic to the nationality of Canada I do not think it would be wise to retain him in our [DOT]employment.

When I say he refused I mean that he refused by neglecting to do so although the matter was brought many times to his attention because he had on several occasions tried to vote and had been challenged, run out of the booth and refused the chance to vote. Thus the matter has been brought very closely to his attention and it certainly must be some inherent dislike to ..Canadian citizenship that lias prevented his becoming naturalized. He has been an active politician outside of voting but he has never been permitted to vote because he would not become a Canadian citizen although reaping all the benefits of Canadian citizenship.
I will look into the matter carefully.

What will the total cost of the St. Louis exhibition be ?
Mr. FISHER, I am informed that we have spent in the neighbourhood of $125,000 for the past fiscal year and that the total cost will be between $275,000 and $300,000 according to expectation.
Is not that very much larger than was anticipated ?

I think, speaking from memory, that I estimated it would be about $250,000 to $275,000.
For the branch of the Commissioner of Agriculture and Dairying, including live stock, dairy, cold storage, extension of markets, poultry, seed and fruit division ; employee* paid from this sum not to be subject to the Civil Service Act, $220,000.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
The day before yesterday when we were discussing poultry stations and chicken feeding, I understood the minister to say that the poultry, owing to the experimental way in which they were fed and marketed, realized 10, 12, and 15 cents per pound. Now I find in the Auditor General's Report, that from the Alberton station, P.E.I., there were sold to Montreal 321 pounds, for $16.05 of these specially fed, scientifically killed chickens, packed In a crate knd sent in cold storage to Montreal, realizing 5 cents a pound. From Mount Stewart, P.E.I., there were sent 52 cases to Great Britain, 2,466 pounds, realizing $236.15, or a fraction over 9 cents per pound, less freight and all expenses. Of 433 pounds of poultry from Rogersville. N.B., 201 pounds were sold in Montreal, realizing $10.05, or 5 cents per pound. From Bondville, Que., 11 cases were sold in Montreal, 558 pounds, realizing $40.26, or 7 cents per pounds, after deducting freight expenses. From Chicoutimi there were fourteen cases sold to Great Britain, 557 pounds, for $33.25, or 6 cents and a fraction per pound. Holmesville, Ont. -my hon. friend dilated for a long time on the great showing made by Holmesville-1 see there wei'e 59 cases, containing 750 chickens, weighing 2,617 pounds, sold in Great Britain and realizing $971)2, or 31 cents per pound. Now, any old woman in the country, catching a scrub chicken, twisting its neck her own way, could pluck the (feathers off it and sell it for a good deal more than these chickens that were killed scientifically, packed in crates, put in cold storage and sent to Great Britain and sold for 3J cents per pound.	Renfrew-I am
sorry my hon. friend from Renfrew (Mr. Wright) is not here ; I find in the Auditor General's Report D-112 what was done at Renfrew. There were sold to Great Britain twelve cases, 625 pounds, for $43.84, or 7 cents per pound. That is what the chickens brought raised in Renfrew. Now these are just a few samples, and I want the minister to explain why he made the statement the day before yesterday with regard to the chickens that were experimented on, when some of them did not bring as much as the cost of their food, to say nothing about any other expenses ; they did not realize as much money as was paid out for the chickens and for the food they ate. Why, these chickens sent from Holmesville to Great Britain only brought 3} cents per pound.

It must be either that the chickens were spoiled after being scientifically fed, or in the killing process their necks were broken the wrong way. Something must have damaged the flavour of the meat, or it would have brought more than that; or it was perhaps the defective cold storage of the hon. gentleman. I want the hon. gentleman to explain how that came about.

He might also remember the statement he made yesterday, which was supported by the hon. member for Renfrew (Mr. Wright), that owing to the splendid way the chickens were fattened, the attractiveness of the food to the human family, the market had been wonderfully increased, and people were consuming much more ; the market had increased and the chickens realized a larger price.

I have not got the details here to show why some of these lots were sold at those low prices. But right alongside of them my hon. friend will see there are other instances where chickens did sell at 12 and 13 cents a pound. I have not got the details of these sales at low prices. There must have been something wrong, but what it was I cannot tell. What I read the other night was a statement of those men who had sold at the prices indicated, who had watched the operation of these stations, and had themselves sold the chickens at the prices I gave. The chickens were fattened on the principles taught at those stations, which these gentlemen themselves had managed successfully in that way. There must be some explanation for the low prices, perhaps in regard to the export, or something of that kind.
Was the station in Prince Edward Island in charge of a man named Haszard, who is now the hon. member for West Queen's ?

That station was not in charge of Mr. Haszard. It was in charge of a Charlottetown gentleman who was recommended by Mr. Haszard to run that station, and for a little while the accounts of the station went through Mr. Haszard's hands. But he ,was not then a member of the House. Because the accounts went through his hands for a little while his name appears in the Auditor General's Report. As a matter of fact he was simply the medium of communication between the department and the man who was doing the work at that station.
Is that man still in charge ; I think he was not a very successful operator ?
That station is closed and I believe the man who had charge of it is doing business on his own account.
The same business.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)

speechtext: Yes, fattening and selling chickens.
The cost of that station was $290 and the return $6. I hope he will do better than that on his own account.
If the hon. gentleman had the full information he would'find the circumstances different.
That is what the Auditor General's Report showed.
Yes, but the Auditor General's Report closes on the 30th of June, and while the expenditure appears one year the receipts would appear in the next year.

That does not account for it, because for two or three years in succession the expenditure has been very much larger than the receipts. Yesterday the minister told us with a flourish of trumpets that his cold storage was perfection, and that the method adopted for fattening chickens was perfection, but now we find that the chickens fattened at Holmesville under his scientific system were sold in England for three and a half cents per pound, so that either the cold storage or the fattening process is a failure. Will the hon. member for Huron (Mr. Holmes) explain 1
Is it the intention of the department to continue the chicken fattening stations as heretofore ?

Yes. Occasionally we close some up and then we start another in a different locality so as to educate the people in the vicinity of each station, and in some cases the men in charge go into business on their own account. I have promised to start one or two in Manitoba, and one or two in British Columbia next year in compliance with the wishes of the people, who are anxious to have them.
How many stations are now in operation ?
Seventeen.
What was the revenue from, and the expenditure on these stations last year 1
That would have to be figured out.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I can give my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) the information. According to the Auditor General's Report these seventeen stations cost last year $14,929.49 ; the revenue from them was $4,327.85 and the net loss to the country $10,601.64.
That's a splendid lesson for the farmers of the country.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
More than that; taking the cost of the feed and the cost of the chickens, not including labour or any other

expense, the loss was $2,693.66. At Holmes-ville, there was a difference between the sales and the cost of the chickens and the feed of $363. We are told that this is accounted. for because the chickens had their necks twisted the wrong way and they sold for only three and three-quarter cents per pound in England. At Bondville, P.Q., the cost of chickens and feed was $889,' the sales brought $485, and the loss $404. The Bondville chickens sold for five cents a pound in Montreal and some shipped to England from Holmesville brought only three and three-quarter cents to seven and a half cents per pound. This proves that either the cold storage or the fattening system is defective.

No one ought expect that the work of these stations should be covered by the sales, but there is some justification for what the hon. gentleman' (Mr. Taylor) says. I believe it is correct to say that in some cases the chickens have not sold for as much as the food and the first cost of the chickens. I have been inquiring and I have found that there have been mistakes made and some leakages. The management of some of these stations cannot be allowed to continue. I do not expect that the sales of the chickens will cover the teaching and illustration work, but they certainly should pay for the prime cost and the cost of the feed. There is no question about that; there is no excuse for anything else and I am now having it thoroughly investigated to see just where the leakage is. It is abundantly possible to buy chickens in the ordinary markets from the farmers, fatten them, and sell them at a profit. That has been done over and over again in these stations. There are instances in which it has not been done.
I believe that in some cases they have bought poor chickens. In other cases they have been incited by competition to buy too many chickens and to pay too much for them. The proper control has not been exercised over these operations ; but I expect to correct that, so that such instances as my hon. friend has cited will not be found in future. But I think it is important that the work should go on in the country, because I know how successful it has been in many ways, and how it has resulted in a very large increase in poultry production, and a considerable increase in profit to a large number of farmers and poultry owners who have followed the lines of this work.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)

speechtext:
I think they must have fed these chickens on sawdust and starved them to death. I am surprised that the minister is not almost ashamed of himself, after the glowing speech he made yesterday about the wonderful development there was in the poultry trade of this country owing to the splendid lessons which had been given to the farmers by these chicken stations, and the increased price at which poultry had been sold as a result of being scientifically fattened. He made out that the consumption had been immensely increased because the chickens were so much more appreciated. He had told the farmers of this country that he wanted to go into a new line which would only cost them $14,929. and yet the very first year there is a loss of $10,000 out of the $15,000 expended-two-thirds of the whole sum, besides all the labour which went for nothing. What a wonderful sense of gratitude the farmers of Canada ought to have toward the Minister of Agriculture for these chicken-fattening stations. It seems to me that one of two things accounts for the result-either that the system is bad or that the cold storage is bad. We were treated to a glowing description of the cold storage, which was represented to be the very best that could be devised ; yet the chickens were sold at 3f cents a pound when an old woman can bring chickens to the market from the barnyard, where they are not fattened at all, and sell them at 8 cents or 9 cents, or 10 cents a pound. I want to point out that at each of the experimental farms there is a chicken branch and a professor of poultry. What is he doing ? He is teaching the farmers the best breeds for laying purposes and the best breeds for fattening. All these farms are experimenting along these lines and every year their reports give the results of these experiments. We thought that was enough. A couple of thousands of dollars a year are

spent at the Central farm for this purpose, and I do not know how mueh at the other farms. Why should this work he dupli- 1 cated ? The hon. minister is starting another system of chicken stations and experimenters all over the country, so that at each place a good supporter can get $300 or $400 for amusing himself by fattening , chickens that sell at cents or 3J cents a pound. We have reports from the experimental farms distributed to the farmers of the country, containing presumably the very knowledge we are trying to get from individuals in various parts of the country. Is it necessary to squander the public money in this way ? For every dollar of return to the people they spend $3, of which $2 have gone to the government supporter or gone to waste in order to show how you can fatten chickens at a loss every time. What kind of a lesson is that to give to the farmers of the country ? Will they thank the government for it ? Will they regard the Minister of Agriculture or those under him as' adepts in the chicken business ? I do not think they will. The very disclosures which have been made are the strongest argument that the money used for this purpose is thrown away, and that the boasted cold storage which we have heard so much about is a failure as well. There is no doubt whatever of this, as otherwise more would have been realized from these stations. Take the chickens on an ordinary farm that are running about picking up refuse and comparatively speaking not fed at all, they are sold at better prices and yield more profitable returns.

Is it the policy of the hon. gentleman to continue keeping up these fattening stations ? It seems to me that when a fattening station has been in operation in any locality for two or three years, the farmers there ought to have learned all they cam from the process, and these stations might very well be abandoned. Take the station at Holmesville, and the figures show the expenditure last year $2,793.19 and the revenue $554.57, leaving a deficit of $2,229,22. If this station be established for educational purposes, my hon. friend who represents that county has not been very well educated. Of course he is occupying the chair and I do not want to say very much about him, but he told the House that the people up there were delighted with it, and that before these chicken fattening stations were put in operation, chickens were sold at about five cents a pound, whereas now they are sold at ten cents a pound. But it appears that the chickens fattened in the very establishment to which he was referring were sold at three and three-quarter cents a pound. It therefore does not look as if the policy adopted by the Minister of Agriculture was very educational in its effect.

The poultry business has undoubtedly been stimulated by the establishment of these stations. There is a larger number of birds raised and fattened than ever before, and as a rule the prices are higher because these birds are better fattened. The hon. gentleman has made a suggestion which is quite in line with what we have been doing. As a general rule these fattening stations are not carried on for more than two or three years in certain localities. But in Holmesville and in one or two places in Prince Edward Island and the province of Quebec, we have breeding stations. We have found by a series of experiments that the birds we raise do better than those we buy for fattening purposes, and we therefore have been breeding birds of a particular type; and as a matter of fact, last season a large number were sold for breeding purposes instead of being fattened. Over 2,000 were thus sold. My hon. friend from Leeds (Mr. Taylor) has hit the nail on the head to a certain extent, because we have been trying, to encourage the breeding of this type and have probably been selling them too cheap.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: They do not cost anything to raise.

It costs something to raise them. But we find there is always a strong request to us not to close a station once it is started, and I have perhaps not been as strict in that respect as I ought to be and hope to be in future. '

Is it a good plan to have so many of these establishments ? If the stations" on the experimental farm are carried on on the same lines and the information disseminated through bulletins, our farmers will get all the information they need in that way.
|Mr. FISHER. I think that the object lessons furnished by these stations has done a great deal of good.

I am unable to see how that can be. If a farmer were to follow the example set by the government, he would soon find himself in the poorhouse, and the only lesson he would take from these stations would be to avoid what is being done there because their experiments result in a loss. I think it is radically wrong that we should not only keep up these stations on our experimental fawns, but duplicate them all over the country. There is evidently a great leak somewhere, and it is about time that it was found out, because year by year this thing instead of getting better is getting worse. It seems to me it is about time to drop the business and come down to common sense.

I know something i about the business in Prince Edward Island.
1 Whether or not the stations there are pay-

ing, is not the question. It is true there is quite a difference between the receipts obtained from the chickens fattened and sold according to the methods followed at tnese experimental stations and the expenditure, but the stations were not established to make money, rather to educate the people in this line of business. I know that the farmers of Prince Edward Island, where these fattening stations are in existence, are now raising a better breed of chickens and making more money. The local market has been very much improved. The price in the Charlottetown market is now fully 100 per cent more than it was a few years ago.
What is the price now '(

A pair of chickens last year was bringing in the local market from 80 cents to ?1. A few years ago they would sell at from 40 cents to 50 cents. Ac to the receipts from these chicken fattening stations, I know that in some cases a breed of chickens was purchased for the purpose of showing that it would not be profitable to raise them. It was not intended to make a profit in every case. I know also that whatever may he said as to beneficial results from the fattening of chickens at the experimental farm, the farmers where these illustration stations are carried on have obtained very much benefit through them, and would be very much opposed to having them closed. Whether the expense is too great or not, that may be a question for discussion. But I have not the slightest doubt that, whatever the direct results, the indirect results in the way of benefits to the farmers are very marked, and as the farmers do not get much in the way of protection or bounties, I think Ithat all they get in this way we should not begrudge them.
As the hon. gentleman is so sure of the beneficial results, can he tell us how many farmers in his section have adopted the cramming process ?
I know that they are raising a better breed of chickens.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Are they feeding with cramming machines ?
They are paying more attention to raising and feeding. The business is very much improved.
In the county from which I come there is not one of these stations so far as I know. Yet the quantity oi chickens raised is about ten times as great as it was a couple of years ago.
You do not want a station there ; you are getting along well enough without it.

I am showing that the development of the poultry trade is not due to the information disseminated by means of these chicken fattening stations, because
whe(re that information Jias never been acted upon the development is quite as great as it is elsewhere. The best evidence that this information is not acted upon is the fact that not many farmers have adopted the cramming process. I would ask the hon. gentleman {Mr. J. J. Hughes) if he can point to one man in his section who has adopted that process ?

If the committee will bear with me for a moment and will permit a digression from the chicken question, I would like to refer to a statement with regard to Mr. Eastman, who is engaged at the St. Louis exhibition. The statement is made that he is an American citizen. I wish to correct that statement, and say that Mr Eastman has lived in the province of New Brunswick for upwards of thirty-five years, that he has been engaged in the lumber business, that he is a man of the highest character, and that he is a naturalized British subject.
When was-he naturalized';

Within the last two or three years. I had to do with his naturalization papers myself and know the circumstances. I think it due to that gentleman and to the committee that the information should be given.
Did he get naturalized to vote for the hon. gentleman (Mr. Einmer-son) or to get this position 1

He had neither object in view,' I fancy. His family is established here, and he wished to claim all the rights of a British subject. I am sure my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) will not feel angry at the fact. I should think, rather, he would rejoice.

I am pleased to know that after thirty-five years Mr. Eastman was convinced that it was the part of wisdom to become a British subject. But the statement was made that he was sent out of a polling place and refused the right to vote because he was not a British subject by birth or naturalization.

He could not be sent out of a polling place under those circumstances, because he never sought to vote until he was naturalized. I am familiar with his personal history and with his relations to the politics of the country. He is a man of the highest character ; treasurer for the province of New Brunswick of the High Court of Foresters ; known and very highly respected all over the province, and a prominent business man connected with the lumber industry.
Not a word was said against his character, and there was no desire to reflect upon it. The question was simply whether he was a British subject.

He is not the man to seek to vote, unless he had the right to

vote, and X contradict the insinuation or tlie statement made against him.

The hon. member from Prince Edward Island (Mr. J. J. Hughes) has given us a lecture on the benefits to the farmers of his section resulting from the chicklen fattening stations. He spoke of it as a protection to the farmers of Prince Edward Island. If it is a protection to the farmers of Prince Edward Island and it does not pay expenses that means that other parts of the country have to pay for the protection given to his constituents. Is there one of these stations that last year received enough from sales to pay for the chickens and the feed, to say nothing of other expenses ?
I have not the figures under my hand, but I am informed that several of them did.
I would ask the hon. member for Prince Edward Island whether any of the stations in bis section paid for the chickens and the feed ?
I have not the figures.

I am assured by those who have looked into the matter that not one of these stations have received enough from chickens sold to pay for the chickens and the feed that went to fatten them. This may be a protection to the people of Prince Edward Island, but is it fair to the rest of the Dominion ? It is surely unfair for one section to ask another section to pay for its benefits through a scheme that is established for the advantage of a few people who are supporting the party in power. This scheme has been a failure so far as making money is concerned, and if the people who are educated by these experiments follow the example of the people carrying on the experiments, it will certainly nor add to our national wealth.
Why should they start any more V We have in Ontario a splendid agricultural college and an agricultural farm for experimental purposes, and any one who wants to learn how to feed and fatten chickens can easily get the reports from that college, without it being necessary to duplicate these establishments all through the country. I think it is the duty of each province to start an agricultural farm and run it as its own expense. Now since the Minister of Agriculture has made a fair test of his business, I do not think it is in the interest of the farming community that he should continue it. Taking into consideration the cost of the test, the rent of the buildings, and all these things, he now knows for a certainty that chickens have not brought in any year the cost of their purchase and their feed ; and yet he wants to bleed the country to the tune of a good many more thousand dollars to establish these stations in other places. I know very well that where he starts a feeding station Mr EMMERSON.
no Tory need apply for a position; but when it comes to paying the deficit each Tory has to pay his share. Now I would ask the Minister of Agriculture to drop these experiments since he has found them a failure. He acknowledged a while ago that the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor) had struck the nail on the head when he said there was a leakage somewhere in giving out the fowl. I venture to say uo Tory got those chickens at less than they are worth.
Lots of them.
If they were given away they were given away the same as appointments-to political friends.
They were not given away, they were sold to anybody that came along.
For less than they were worth ?
For less than they would have fetched if we had tried to sell them for a high price. Our object was to disseminate the breed throughout the country.

In Ontario all we have to do is to look up the records of what is done in the Agricultural College at Guelph, and we can certainly do as well fattening chickens there as the hon. gentleman. I would ask him as an honest representative of the farmers, after be has tested this business and found it a failure, to drop it.

I notice one thing peculiar about these experimental stations. There are three in the province of Ontario, and every one of them is in a Reform riding. One would imagine if they are to continue for the province of Ontario there should be some of these stations in Conservative ridings.
Perhaps the Reform members look better after their constituents.

Perhaps the hon. minister hears them better when they call. I see one at Bowmanville, in the county of Durham, represented by a good supporter of the present government. Another is in the county of West Huron, rather a noted county in western Ontario.
A distinguished county.
The other is in Renfrew.
Another distinguished county.

Perhaps they will be a little more distinguished after the next general election. But it does seem a little strange that these three establishments for the province of Ontario should be found in three Reform ridings. My hon. friend said he was selling these chickens cheap to the farmers, I hope he will not take advantage of

that practice when the election comes along. I think the minister will not deny that the chickens sold by the farmers generally in the province of Ontario are equal in every respect and bring as high a price as those from these establishments. For myself I do not think that these establishments so managed are in the interests of the people of Canada, but if the hon. gentleman thinks they are, he should distribute them more fairly, instead of confining them to Reform ridings.

X have the greatest respect for the hon. gentleman who has just spoken (Mr. Blain) and for the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule), but I do not share in the views they have expressed on this question. I am quite prepared to consent that in all these experimental matters we should pay out more money than we receive. If the minister could not account for the difference between the net receipts for the chickens and the expense for their food, I would have some hesitation in supporting the continuance of the experiment. But the minister has accounted for the deficiency. He has annnounced in the most definite way that this industry can be carried on in a manner that will make it ultimately profitable, and I believe that is the case. I do not think, however, the hon. minister has been as candid as he ought to have been, because the announcement he has made to-night he could have made last night when the same subject was before the House. I think we may now accept his statement that the shortage comes, not from the fact that a profit cannot be made, but from the fact that there has been mismanagement, and probably something worse than mismanagement in these matters. Now I suggest that the government shall continue 'these experiments. I believe there is an enormous demand for chickens. I believe that money can be made out of the business, and X believe in opening up all the avenues of industry and profitable investment in this country, and as this is one of those industries which is directly connected with the farm. X would like to see it continued. I want it continued in the future upon a proper business basis. The minister has admitted that there has been a leakage in this matter. He says that he does not believe it results from any favouritism. I do not care how it has happened, I think it should be prevented. This branch of the experimental work should be continued and in the future it may be made a profitable branch of the work. I think it is right to experiment in regard to this- industry and I think that notwithstanding what has been said by the hon. member for Peel the farmers will approve of the expenditure of money upon this experiment but they will hold the government of course to an honest and careful expenditure of money
even though it is for experimental purposes.

We are doing all this work at the farm and are sending out every year from 50,000 tb 100,000 bulletins containing this information. I do not think we should duplicate any of this work. Why should these fattening stations be maintained; especially when out of every three dollars you put in them you lose two ?

I can easily understand how the hon. member for Prince Edward Island (Mr. J. J. Hughes) or any other member from a county where a fattening sltation is operated should be in favour of them. These stations provide a home market for these farmers for their chickens, and of course a home market is always the best. The fattening station takes up all the chickens from the surrounding country at a good price without any trouble to the farmers so of course they are in favour of it. But people who live in other parts of the country do not profit from the establishment of these stations as do the hon. member's supporters. In the county of Huron, of course, the station at Holmes-ville furnishes a home market for the chickens raised in that county and takes them off the hands of the farmers without any expense or trouble.

It seems to me that the system of fattening chickens adopted by the Minister of Agriculture is rather getting away from the legitimate mode of farming operations. I think myself that the business of the farmer is to raise chickens, to raise as many as he can. In this the government can very materially assist him by having at all times a supply of the eggs of the best breeds of poultry not only for laying purposes but for food. Let the farmers be encouraged in every way possible by providing a full supply of eggs of the varieties that are most approved of, for the purposes of the fattening stations. I know in the section of country from which I come this process of stuffing chickens is not in vogue. I have not heard of its being adopted by any one, but I have known a person with a large poultry yard who desired to get rid of his whole flock to find no difficulty in selling them all, live weight, at 10 cents a pound. That I think is a great deal better than fattening and stuffing and selling them at 7 cents or even 10 cents a pound dead weight. I have an idea that it would be much better and more profitable to encourage the farmer to raise the chickens and sell them to professional chicken fatteners. You will find in large places such as Toronto, companies which will do this class of work. In Toronto I know there is a large company which will take all the chickens they can secure within a radius of some 30 or 40 miles of that city.

At the fattening stations we do about the business the hon. gentle-

man speaks of, that is we buy the chickens from the farmers and fatten them. At the rearing stations we do that partly and we also raise them from eggs in order to compare the results from chickens raised on the spot and fed from birth and those which are picked up from farmers around. At the breeding stations we have been breeding birds which we think especially adapted for fattening purposes and also selling breeding eggs. That is the educational work that has been going on and largely as a result of what we have been doing the market in Toronto has vastly improved. I do not claim credit for the whole of it, but I do say that since we have commenced this fattening and preparing for market, and since attention has been directed to it, it has been constantly increasing and there is a very large market.
I think it is a matter that should be left largely to private enterprise. Are there any other fattening establishments throughout Canada such as I have described at Toronto.
There are one or two others, but I think this is the best.
When the supplementary estimates come down we will want further information on cold storage, fruit, seed, and some other matters.
I will be glad to give the information.
You had better not give it to-night, because it will take you till seven o'clock to-morrow morning. You can give it on the suplementary estimates.
Very well.
We will also want some information about this ' extension of markets.'

Very well.
Some resolutions reported.
Mr. FIELDING moved the adjournment of the House.
What business will be taken up on Monday ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The adjournment was rather earlier than I expected, and I had no opportunity to see the premier. I think I may safely say that we will continue in supply, and probably with the railway estimates.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 9.35 p.m.
Monday, July 25, 1904.
